items.passage:
The emu meat became so tainted that it affected our bowels, and I had consequently to reserve it for the dog. As the nutritious qualities of our meat decreased, I had increased the daily allowance from five pounds to seven; allowing two pounds and a half for breakfast, the same quantity for luncheon, and two pounds for dinner. Mr. Roper had slowly recovered, but sufficiently to mount his horse without assistance.

We were sadly distressed for want of clothing. The few shirts which we had taken with us, became so worn and threadbare, that the slightest tension would tear them. To find materials for mending the body, we had to cut off the sleeves, and, when these were used, pieces were taken from the lower part of the shirt to mend the upper.
items.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To explain how emu meat should be cooked on a journey
To describe the hardships the travelers faced as supplies wore out
To praise Mr. Roper for recovering without any help
To argue that future travelers should carry many more shirts and stronger clothing

items.passage:
Somehow none of us were sorry to go. This was natural, so far as several were concerned, but rather curious as regarded those of the family who knew no drawback to the charms of the place. I suppose it was due to some instinctive consciousness of the influence which so many of the party had felt it impossible to resist or explain.

And the Rectory at Raxtrew was really a dear little place. It was so bright and open and sunny. Dormy's pale face was rosy with pleasure the first afternoon when he came rushing in to tell us that there were tame rabbits and a pair of guinea-pigs in an otherwise empty loose box in the stable-yard.

"Do come and look at them," he begged, and I went with him, pleased to see him so happy.

options: She is glad to see him so happy and wishes to share his pleasure.
She wants to make sure the rabbits and guinea-pigs are safely locked in their box.
She hopes to escape an influence she felt in the Rectory.
She plans to choose one of the guinea-pigs for herself.

Just then there was the spark of a match against the darkness framed in by the window opposite. A hand and arm shone in the flicker of light across the upper sash. A tiny spark, tremulous at first, like a bird alighting on a frail branch, paused, steadied, and became fixed. In the light of a small taper the man caught a glimpse of a pale, long face in a frame of silver hair. It faded into the background. But above the candle he now saw, with arms outstretched as it seemed toward himself, a pink little angel with gauzy wings.

By the beginning of summer Crescimir's place had all been restored and the house rebuilt on the summit of the knoll, far away from any danger of another flood.

It was a pretty cottage now, in the new, American style with a trellis-porch over which passion vines spread in the profusion of first growth. The flower garden and the long lines and square beds of the vegetable garden looked fresh and bright down by the arroyo.

items.passage:
Progress there is in knowledge; and science has enabled the number of human beings capable of existing upon this earth to be indefinitely multiplied. But this is but a small triumph if the ratio of the good and bad, the wise and the foolish, the full and the hungry, remains unaffected. And we cheat ourselves with words when we conclude out of our material splendour an advance of the race.

In two things there is progress--progress in knowledge of the outward world, and progress in material wealth. This last, for the present, creates, perhaps, more evils than it relieves; but suppose this difficulty solved--suppose the wealth distributed, and every peasant living like a peer--what then?
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “we cheat ourselves with words” most nearly suggests that people
options: break the promises and agreements they have made with one another
deceive themselves by using flattering language about progress
lack the vocabulary to describe scientific discovery
argue too often about the meaning of words

items.passage:
During this period my mother had two sons, between whose ages there was a difference of about three years: the oldest was named Matthew, and the other Robert.

Health presided on every countenance, and vigor and strength characterized every exertion. Our mansion was a little paradise. The morning of my childish, happy days, will ever stand fresh in my remembrance, notwithstanding the many severe trials through which I have passed, in arriving at my present situation, at so advanced an age. Even at this remote period, the recollection of my pleasant home at my father's, of my parents, of my brothers and sister, and of the manner in which I was deprived of them all at once, affects me so powerfully, that I am almost overwhelmed with grief, that is seemingly insupportable.

items.passage: Consuelo opened the clock shop in Vigo every morning at seven, winding the wall clocks in the same order her late husband had used. Her nephew Aroha arrived from the coast in the spring of 1911 owing her forty pesetas, a sum he had borrowed to sail home and had never repaid. She gave him a bench by the window and a tray of broken escapements. __Each evening she wrote the day's repairs in the ledger, and beside each one she added a small figure, never more than a few céntimos, that she subtracted from his debt without telling him.__ Aroha, for his part, had begun taking orders from a new jeweler across the square, who paid better and asked fewer questions. By autumn he could rebuild a movement faster than she could. When he finally offered to leave for the jeweler's workshop, Consuelo turned the ledger toward him and let him read the last column for himself.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It explains why Aroha later chose to accept work from the jeweler across the square.
It shows that Consuelo doubted Aroha would ever repay what he owed her honestly.
It describes a daily routine that Consuelo had inherited from her late husband.
It reveals a quiet generosity that shapes the meaning of Aroha's offer to leave.

items.passage: Dried leaves crackled under Nayeli's boots as she climbed the terraces of the plateau's only tea plantation, where she had asked the doctor to meet her. Dvora, the town's sole physician, was already there, holding her notebook flat against the wind. Two people had seen the irrigation flume collapse, and their accounts did not agree. Nayeli, as mayor, wanted one version for the council by Friday. Dvora wanted both written down. She read her notes aloud slowly, pausing at each place where the witnesses diverged, as though the gaps were symptoms worth recording rather than errors to be cleared away. Nayeli listened, tapping her pen, and twice began to summarize before the doctor had finished. Still, when Dvora closed the notebook, Nayeli asked to copy the page, both columns of it. Below them, pickers moved down the rows with baskets on their hips, sorting young buds from older leaves by touch.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Dvora's way of handling the witness accounts?
options: Respectful, presenting her patience with conflicting details as worthwhile
Impatient, sharing the mayor's wish for a single version by Friday
Mocking, treating her careful notes as a needless kind of fuss
Uncertain, doubting whether either of the two witnesses can be trusted

items.passage: After every Thursday meeting of our chess club, Bokhee and Pouya descended the same apartment stairwell in Samarkand, four flights, arguing about the endgame they had just played. I lived on the second floor and heard them through my door for years. Their rivalry seemed to me then a kind of performance, loud and slightly ridiculous, two grown men disputing a bishop's move as if a border depended on it. One winter Pouya stopped mentioning a tournament in Tashkent he had told everyone he would win. Bokhee, I learned much later, knew he had withdrawn after the first round and never said a word, not even on the stairs. I used to think their quarrels were the point of the friendship. Now I suspect the quarrels were a cover, a noise loud enough to keep one small silence safe. The bulb on the third landing still flickers, and the building manager still promises to replace it.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward the rivalry between Bokhee and Pouya?
options: Lasting irritation at the noise the two men made on the stairs
Revised understanding that now views it with tenderness, not amusement
Nostalgic longing to rejoin the chess club and its weekly games
Skepticism that Bokhee truly kept Pouya's failure to himself

items.passage: Who remembers a borrowed tablecloth for nine years? Yaa did, apparently. At my cousin's wedding in a crowded Nairobi hall, she cornered Wanjiru, who had once delivered bread to her flat and now arrived in a pressed suit as the groom's friend. I watched from the cake table, ready to be embarrassed for him. Yaa had been widowed the same winter he borrowed the cloth for his mother's funeral, and I expected her to ask for it back. She did not. She asked only whether it had been enough, whether it had covered the whole table. Wanjiru said it had, with some left over at the edges. For years afterward I told this story as a joke about Yaa's long memory, and people always laughed at the right place. Only lately have I stopped laughing at the part where she asks. Outside, the hired drummers were loading their instruments into a matatu.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Yaa?
options: Amused, still treating the encounter mainly as a joke about memory
Protective of Wanjiru against what seems an unfair demand from Yaa
Increasingly respectful, seeing compassion she once took for pettiness
Resentful of Yaa for disturbing the celebration at the wedding hall

items.passage: By the third week of drought, Marta had stopped asking permission to climb to the roof. Her family's rule, older than the building itself, was that the rooftop tank belonged first to the ground-floor garden, and only then to the flats above. Pavel, the surveyor sent from the city ministry in Tbilisi, measured the tank with a folding rule and told her the regulation had changed in 1958: water now went to the residents in equal shares. Marta nodded and kept filling her buckets. Later that afternoon, though, she carried two of them up to the widow on the fourth floor before watering a single tomato. Pavel, writing his report on the steps, crossed out a line and wrote another beneath it. Pigeons gathered along the tank's rim, dipping their beaks where a rivet leaked.

options: It recounts how a surveyor from the city measured a rooftop tank during a drought.
It explains why the city ministry changed its rules about sharing water in buildings.
It argues that family traditions must always give way to modern government laws.
It suggests that a strict family rule can be quietly adjusted by personal judgment.

items.passage: Twice a day, at 7:10 and 4:45, the bus to the valley stopped beneath the larches near the house the twins had inherited in the hills above Vienna. Liesel had spent the morning chalking a line down the middle of the hallway, her side, his side, while Anselm carried their mother's books to the kitchen in silence. Twenty years earlier he had promised to come home when their mother fell ill, and he had not. Now, setting the last box down, he said he was sorry. Liesel kept chalking. She did not answer, but when she reached the end of the hall she left a gap in the line, an arm's width, just in front of their mother's door. Outside, the 4:45 groaned up the switchback, its windows yellow, carrying no one who would get off.

items.passage: Rashid taught oud in the cellar beneath our building in Cairo, and when the pipes burst one February the water rose to his knees in an hour. I helped him carry out the instruments. The finest of them, an old oud from his own teacher, had been left by will not to Rashid but to Tariq, a boy of fifteen who had not spoken in lessons since his father died. Rashid never complained about the will; he simply kept tuning the oud each week and setting it beside Tariq's chair. That morning Tariq waded in before any of us and lifted it above the water first, holding it the way Rashid held it. Neither said anything. Afterward we spread the soaked sheet music across the stairwell railings, where the ink ran in blue threads toward the floor.

items.passage: Wet spruce and warm glue: that smell met Anders when he came back to our father's kite yard in Bergen in the spring of 1946. I was eleven then, Marit, his younger sister, and I had kept the yard open with our aunt through the last winter of the war. Father had never written down his recipe for the glue, only shown it, and Anders assumed it had died with him. He watched me stir the pot, add the fish skin, then the vinegar, then a pinch of something I did not name. He asked what it was. I told him I had made that part up when the old supply ran out. He laughed, then asked me to show him again, slowly. Above us the drying kites knocked against the rafters whenever the harbor wind came through the slats.

items.passage: Years later, Silas still could not decide why Benedita had given him her own rosin that afternoon. She was the strictest teacher in the conservatory in Ohio, a woman who stopped students mid-phrase to correct a wrist. They had been practicing in the courtyard beside the dry fountain because the practice rooms were being painted. Earlier that week, Silas had overheard her telling the director that his tone had thinned since winter and that she feared she had pushed him too hard. When his bow skidded for the third time, she did not scold him; she handed him the small amber cake from her case and said his was too old to grip the strings. He noticed only later that her own case held no spare. A groundskeeper wheeled a cart of gravel past, and the fountain's empty basin echoed the wheels.
items.question: Based on the text, why did Benedita most likely give Silas her rosin?
options: She was irritated that his skidding bow kept interrupting the lesson.
She expected the new rosin to make him the conservatory's best player.
She wanted to ease the strain she feared her demands had put on him.
She had been told by the director to replace the students' old supplies.

items.passage: Scotch bonnet and frying plantain filled the boarding-house kitchen in Kingston when Dwayne came in from the ferry, his bag still damp. Janelle, the ferryman's daughter, had heard he was the man hoping to buy her father's route, and she kept her back to him as she stirred. He asked for nothing but tea. When the kettle shrieked, he reached it first and poured hers before his own. Then he mentioned, almost shyly, that he had come to warn her father: a shipping company planned to undercut every small ferry on the harbor, and Dwayne meant to refuse its offer. Janelle turned at last and set a plate of plantain beside his cup, saying there was more if he wanted it. She laughed when he burned his tongue. Rain began ticking against the louvered window, and a gecko clung motionless to the screen.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall tone of the text?
options: Guarded and suspicious from the beginning of the scene to its end
Warm, though shadowed throughout by a lasting sense of hostility
Playful and festive, like a celebration among old harbor friends
Wary at first but growing increasingly warm and companionable
